analysis.one_liner: Requires coal mining companies to post real cleanup bonds instead of promising to pay for their own mine reclamation.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 26, 2026 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee; no hearing or vote has been scheduled and only 3 House members sponsor it.
analysis.plain_summary: When a coal company goes bankrupt without setting aside enough money, taxpayers often foot the bill for restoring the stripped mine land it leaves behind. This bill would tighten the federal mine cleanup bonding rules: companies could no longer 'self-bond' — that is, promise to pay cleanup costs out of their own finances — and would instead have to buy real bonds or post collateral. It would also require states using alternative cleanup funds to prove those funds are financially sound, and set rules to keep surety companies from issuing bonds they cannot back.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and state taxpayers, who currently absorb cleanup costs when a coal operator walks away from a mine with an inadequate bond; and residents of coal states, who would otherwise live next to unrestored mines.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Secretary from accepting a company's own promise to pay (a 'self-bond') as its cleanup bond on federal lands and programs, and directs the Secretary to require states that allow self-bonding to amend their programs to remove that authority [S2].
Requires coal operations already covered by a self-bond to replace it with an acceptable bond at the next permit renewal or major permit modification [S2].

Requires any state alternative bonding system to present a 7-year history of bond forfeitures and reclamation costs, an engineer's estimate of remaining cleanup costs, and a 5-year forecast proving the bond pool will be financially sound [S2].

Directs the Secretary to write rules within one year limiting how many reclamation bonds a single surety can issue in a state and requiring minimum collateralization and cash reserves, so the cleanup promise does not fail with the surety company [S2].

Bars companies from posting coal, mines, or mining equipment as bond collateral, requires re-evaluation of non-liquid collateral every three years, and allows the Secretary to count executive pay as backing for a bond [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining operators, who would have to buy surety bonds or post real collateral instead of relying on their own balance sheets, and in some cases their customers through higher coal prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mining companies and surety costs

drawbacks.text: Bonding costs rise for marginal operators; critics of ending self-bonding argue financially strong companies can safely promise their own cleanup, and the added premiums could push weak mines into bankruptcy sooner — the exact event the bonding system is meant to guard against (general reasoning about how bonding works; the bill text itself does not address this) [S2].

The bill shifts risk from companies to surety insurers; if sureties are thinly capitalized, taxpayers could still be exposed, which the bill addresses only by directing the Secretary to write collateral rules within a year rather than setting hard standards itself [S2].

A company that cannot obtain a bond could lose its permit, so the bill concentrates financial pressure on smaller operators even where reclamation risk is modest (inference from the permit-bonding structure of the amended section) [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The taxpayer protection is real and targeted at a recurring problem: coal company bankruptcies have repeatedly left reclamation bills for the public. The main cost is higher bonding expenses for coal operators, and the bill's protections depend on the Interior Department writing strong surety rules. On balance the benefit to taxpayers outweighs the compliance cost, though the design leans on regulators to get the details right.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote; Congress is still in session, so it is waiting and unlikely to move with only three sponsors.

narrative.text: Summer Lee (D-PA) introduced the bill on May 26, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S4].
The bill's only cosponsors are Reps. Deluzio and Beyer, both Democrats; no Republican has joined [S3].

The bill would amend the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act's bonding section to ban self-bonding, require financial proof for state alternative bonding systems, and set limits on surety bonds and collateral [S2].
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators who would have faced new bonding requirements keep the status quo, and taxpayers continue to carry the risk of covering mine cleanup when companies fail. No one has yet had to change behavior because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators keep the status quo

sides.party_line_note: There has been no vote, and no opposition has acted on the record; all three sponsors are Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill ends self-bonding and requires real bonds or collateral, raising the money coal operators must set aside for cleanup. Their cost is the public's gain, since shortfalls today fall on taxpayers when companies fail.
Requiring third-party bonds creates new business for corporate sureties, though the bill also subjects them to new federal rules on how many bonds they can issue and how much cash they must hold.

analysis.trajectory: With only three sponsors, no Republican support, and no hearing scheduled in the Natural Resources Committee with the Congress ending January 3, 2027, the bill's most likely path is to sit in committee and expire. Bills at this stage rarely move without a committee decision to hold a markup, and nothing in the action history indicates one is planned.
